GXO Logistics is seeing accelerating demand for its contract logistics services, particularly in North America, as data centers, aerospace and defense customers fuel a record sales pipeline.
During a Wednesday earnings call, CEO Patrick Kelleher said the company’s renewed commercial strategy is generating larger contracts and expanding opportunities in specialized industries, with momentum expected to continue into 2027.
“The focus on North America , the focus on the strategic verticals, has been additive to the organic growth agenda,” Kelleher told analysts during the call.
Greenwich, Connecticut-based GXO (NYSE: GXO) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.59 billion, a 5.7% increase from $3.4 billion a year earlier. Organic revenue increased 6.4%, while adjusted earnings per share rose 13% to 89 cents.
The company secured $375 million in new business wins during the quarter, a 34% year-over-year increase, and ended September with a record $3.1 billion sales pipeline, up more than 30%.
He said GXO’s contract logistics business typically operates on a six-month sales cycle, meaning initiatives launched over the past year are only beginning to translate into revenue.
North America, data centers drive expansion
North America has emerged as GXO’s largest growth opportunity , with its regional sales pipeline increasing more than 80% year over year to approximately $1.3 billion.
Chief Strategy Officer Kristine Kubacki said the company’s pipeline across the United Kingdom and Europe reached approximately $1.7 billion.
Technology and consumer electronics were GXO’s fastest-growing customer category during the quarter, with revenue increasing 19%, largely driven by data center activity.
Kelleher said GXO continues to see strong demand from technology companies expanding their data center infrastructure, with no signs of a slowdown in requests for proposals.
The company is also pursuing more business in aerospace and defense, industrial logistics and life sciences. Those strategic growth industries accounted for approximately 40% of GXO’s new business wins through the first nine months of 2026.
Kubacki said contracts involving data centers and aerospace customers often require more complex logistics services than traditional retail and consumer distribution.
“Those are very complex mandates, very complicated supply chains,” Kubacki said. “It tends to be stickier. It tends to be higher value-added services.”
GXO also reported new or expanded business relationships during the quarter with Applied Materials, Boeing, NetApp, Unilever and L’Oréal.
The company expects to enter 2027 with more than $850 million in incremental revenue from previously signed contracts, compared with $774 million entering 2026.
Rapid contract growth pressures margins
While revenue and contract wins accelerated, GXO executives said that the pace of new customer onboarding created additional expenses during the quarter.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization remained flat at $251 million, resulting in a 7% adjusted EBITDA margin .
Kelleher said the company had to bring in outside consulting and implementation resources to support the rapid launch of several large customer operations.
“With organic growth accelerating at the pace it has, we really found ourselves in Q3 stretched in terms of implementation resources,” he said.
Kelleher characterized those additional expenses as specific to the quarter rather than an ongoing structural problem. He said GXO is expanding its internal implementation capabilities to support future growth.
GXO maintains 2026 outlook
Despite the costs associated with expanding operations, GXO reaffirmed its full-year financial guidance.
The company continues to expect organic revenue growth of 4% to 5%, adjusted EBITDA of $945 million to $965 million and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $2.95 to $3.15.
Suchinski said GXO expects fourth-quarter organic growth slightly above 5%, assuming flat customer volumes. However, if stronger demand continues through the holiday shipping season, growth could approach the 6.4% achieved in the third quarter.
Third-quarter operating cash flow declined to $156 million from $232 million a year earlier, while free cash flow fell to $85 million from $187 million.
Suchinski attributed the free cash flow decline primarily to the timing of enterprise resource planning investments and higher net capital expenditures.
GXO expects the fourth quarter to be its strongest cash-generating period of the year.

Net income | $65M | $60M | +8.3%
Adjusted EBITDA | $251M | $251M | Flat
Adjusted diluted EPS | $0.89 | $0.79 | +12.7%

Why it matters: GXO’s results highlight the challenge facing contract logistics providers: scaling operations quickly enough to capture new business without sacrificing margins.

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.
Ford Fathom EV prices range up to the high $30,000s
After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.
Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.
Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.
Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.
When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.
“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.
According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.
“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”
Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
Ford Fathom EV pickup spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Reddit)
We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.
The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.
We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.
Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.
GM recalls Cadillac, Chevy EVs due to a brake software
The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.
After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.
When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.
2027 Cadillac Vistiq (Source: Cadillac)
In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:
2023 – 2027 Cadillac Lyriq
2025 – 2026 Cadillac Celstiq
2026 – 2027 Cadillac Vistiq
2024 – 2027 Chevy Blazer EV
According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.
The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.
2026 Cadillac Lyriq (Source: Cadillac)
GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.
Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.
You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
GM Pulls the Plug on the Corvette SUV Project
8 photos
Photo: Evren Ozgun Spy Sketch | YouTube
General Motors has reportedly pulled the plug on the SUV Corvette that the auto giant was planning to launch as part of a lineup expansion. The project has been shelved until further notice. Translation: until the market becomes more stable.
General Motors has reportedly scrapped plans to expand the Corvette lineup into a standalone sub-brand, putting an end to the development of a long-rumored all-electric crossover SUV , a four-door sedan, and a pure EV sports car.
The decision marks a major strategic shift for the auto giant, which has been quietly working behind the scenes on the ambitious lineup expansion slated to launch around the 2025 - 2026 calendar years and postponed until it was completely canceled.
Codenamed V224, with some sources noting V284, but none officially confirmed, the all-electric crossover was envisioned as a high-volume, high-performance model, aimed directly at the Porsche Cayenne.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, GM Authority reports that the core model variants should have been underpinned by a newly developed premium BEV Prime architecture. The same platform would have been used for an electric two-door sports car .
Photo: Evren Ozgun Spy Sketch | YouTube In the meantime, a four-door electric sedan with a fastback-like silhouette, bearing the Corvette badge and different power versions, was also part of the plan for an end-of-the-decade launch, targeting competition with the Porsche Taycan.
Chevrolet hasn't confirmed the cancellation, as it hasn't disclosed any details when the models were supposedly in development, so there is no official explanation for the move. However, we can easily read between the lines and blame the plunging EV demand, especially in the performance segment, over the past year.
Furthermore, expanding the lineup with models that were unlike anything before it would have been massive cause for backlash. Just remember what Ferrari had to deal with when unveiling its first-ever EV , the Luce , earlier this year, or what Porsche went through when it rolled out its first SUV, the Cayenne, back in 2022.
For the moment, the Corvette lineup remains as you know it, starting with the base Stingray with the 6.2-liter LT2 V8 producing 490 horsepower (497 metric horsepower) and going all the way to the hybrid ZR1X , with its mind-blowing 1,250 horsepower (1,268 metric horsepower).
Photo: Evren Ozgun Spy Sketch | YouTube No EV, no SUV, and no sedan will intrude in the lineup for the moment, as General Motors would rather focus on developing the C9 generation instead of coming up with new models for the C8. However, the C9 won't drop before 2029 as a 2030 model year.
In the meantime, electrification might be contagious for other models of the Corvette portfolio. For the moment, only the Grand Sport X and the ZR1X feature an electric motor and all-wheel drive. GM Authority notes that an electric two-door Corvette project might be very much alive, even though there is no active vehicle program associated with it.

source_document.body:
North American Class 8 truck orders tumbled 36% year over year in October, signaling a surprisingly weak start to the 2027 order season.
Trucking fleets are grappling with regulatory uncertainty , rising equipment costs and pressure on operating margins, according to data released Wednesday by FTR Transportation Intelligence.
Dan Moyer, FTR’s senior analyst for commercial vehicles, said fleets may be shifting their capital spending priorities toward trailers instead of tractors in the near term.
He also noted that higher operating expenses continue to challenge carriers despite improvements in freight pricing.
“Also, while freight rates are strong, so are costs for fuel, insurance, and labor, pressuring margins and possibly limiting purchases for now,” Moyer said.
Preliminary net orders totaled 15,600 units in October, down 24% from September , The October total was nearly 50% below the 10-year average of 31,089 units for the month, underscoring a significant slowdown in heavy-duty truck demand heading into 2027.
Despite the October decline, year-to-date Class 8 orders totaled 278,201 units, up 74% compared with the same period in 2025.
Combined September and October orders reached 36,002 units, down 20% from the comparable period last year, FTR reported.
FTR indicated that underlying conditions continue to support demand for new heavy-duty trucks, despite October’s disappointing results.
Moyer said the earlier wave of truck purchases ahead of anticipated 2027 emissions requirements has already run its course.
“Underlying replacement needs, tighter capacity, and firmer freight rates continue to support Class 8 demand,” Moyer said. “However, with the earlier EPA 2027 pre-buy now complete, orders are increasingly tied to fleet profitability, capital spending priorities, and regulatory certainty.”
FTR also cautioned that October’s weak orders may reflect purchases being delayed rather than eliminated altogether.
“Weak October results suggest that some purchases may be deferred rather than canceled, potentially allowing orders to strengthen as emissions requirements, production schedules, and equipment pricing become clearer,” Moyer said.
Class 8 truck orders — October 2026
Metric | Result
October preliminary net orders | 15,600
Month-over-month change | -24%
Year-over-year change | -36%
10-year October average | 31,089
September–October combined orders | 36,002
September–October YoY change | -20%
2026 year-to-date orders | 278,201
Year-to-date YoY change | +74%
Source: FTR Transportation Intelligence, Nov. 4, 2026. Figures are preliminary North American Class 8 net orders.
Why it matters: The weak start to the 2027 truck-order season raises questions about equipment demand and manufacturers’ production schedules, even as stronger freight rates and replacement needs support the market.

Alfa Romeo's New 2028 Giulia Has BMW DNA, Looks Like a Botched-Up Sports Sedan – Rendering
6 photos
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Theottle
The Alfa Romeo Giulia is in dire need of a makeover, as the current one has been around since 2015, albeit with a mid-cycle refresh that arrived in late 2022 for the 2024 model year, and is meant to keep it on the appealing side of the premium compact sedan class for as long as possible.
And this model will actually stick around for as long as possible, because while its successor it actually in the making, Stellantis admitted that it is “under study.” This information came out earlier this year, in a slide that’s part of the 2030 Stellantis roadmap, which revealed some early information about five upcoming products from Alfa Romeo. The facelifted Junior, a replacement for the Tonale, a premium hatch, Bottega Fuoriserie projects, and a D-segment car were mentioned there.
Certain outlets quote an Alfa Romeo spokesperson, who mentioned “future evolutions of the Giulia and Stelvio in the D-segment.” And this makes us wonder whether the two will get individual successors, with the former still taking on the likes of the BMW 3 Series and the latter attacking the premium compact crossover class, or if these will be merged into a single model. The latter idea may seem like a long stretch, but it actually reveals why there is a single model in the above-mentioned slide and not two of them.
Previous reports suggested that the successor to the current Alfa Romeo Giulia might actually be a fastback crossover, and that information was eventually joined by some patent images sketching out its exterior design. Subsequently, the Italian car marque put the project on ice for now, so trying to decipher what the next-gen Giulia will be and when it will launch is basically mission impossible at this point. The same goes for its platform-sharing sibling, the Stelvio.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Theottle For what it’s worth, the sedan and the crossover will stick around through 2028, and the Quadrifoglio is now back in business. This inevitably tells us that Stellantis, which is Alfa Romeo’s parent company in case you forgot, is trying to play the safe card when it comes to these models, not rushing into anything, and perhaps looking to read these challenging times as they unfold before taking an official decision when it comes to the future of the Giulia and the Stelvio.
But if we basically know nothing about the successor to the otherwise cool albeit aging sports sedan, then what is up with the images shared in the gallery, you ask? Well, they are renderings, and they came from Theottle on YouTube. The pixel artist revealed the creation process in a short clip, which concludes with a few shots of the imagined next-generation Alfa Romeo Giulia, which uses something very unusual as a blank canvas.
We are talking about the BMW 4 Series Gran Coupe , which was used as a foundation stone for these digital illustrations. Mind you, the Alfa product does not exactly look like a 4er, as almost everything has changed, save for the shape of the side windows, the sloping roofline, and a few other bits and bobs.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Theottle The CGI-infused next-gen Alfa Romeo Giulia has a typical Alfa face, with a familiar grille design flanked by the new headlights, a clean bumper at the front, flush door handles, a pair of round taillights, an integrated ducktail spoiler, and an aggressive design overall at the rear. The familiar Alfa Romeo wheels were chosen for this rendered machine, which is not exactly the prettiest next-gen Giulia that we have seen from the pixel-altering crowd, is it?
Then again, it is not the worst either, but the fact that it has been based on a Bimmer makes it a lot less appealing, in this writer’s eyes, anyway. Something like this has zero chances of happening, unless the BMW Group and Stellantis decide to hold hands for whatever reason, but that obviously won’t happen. But do you actually think it would be a good idea for the Giulia’s successor to use the CLAR platform, which, in its current iteration is the foundation stone of the modern-day 3 Series (G50)?
While you wrap your mind around that otherwise silly question, we will remind you that the aging Alfa Romeo Giulia is now in the 2026 model year in the United States of America, and the lineup presented on the company’s official website shows two trim levels. The first one is simply called the Giulia, and the second is known as the Giulia Veloce Package (for obvious reasons), and pricing starts at $44,995 with rear-wheel drive, whereas the all-wheel drive system is a $2,000 optional extra.
Now, what’s your take on the very blurry future of the Alfa Romeo Giulia (and Stelvio)? What about the rendered model with its German DNA? Tell us all about it in the comments area below.

Dodge Debuts the Sub-Zero Paint for Its Durango Bestseller
7 photos
Photo: Dodge
Dodge has just debuted the Sub-Zero paint in the Durango lineup eight months after introducing it for the Charger two-door and four-door, both ICE and EV. It is the 11th exterior option that customers can choose from when they spec their future Durango SUV with a HEMI under the hood.
Sub-Zero drops as a solid blue-gray exterior finish, formulated specifically to deliver two distinct visual personalities based on how the light strikes, Dodge reps explain. The paint appears deep and subtle in the shade, but it is a brighter, cool-tone blue in direct sunlight.
The color debuted on the all-new 2 026 Dodge Charger back in March, becoming available for the entire lineup, regardless of the number of doors or powertrain. Eight months later, it was ported into the Durango lineup as Dodge is trying to make its aging SUV more attractive. The third generation of the third-row SUV has been on the market since 2010, when it was launched as a 2011 model year.
The introduction of Sub-Zero expands the configuration possibilities of the flagship Durango SRT Hellcat Jailbreak. Dodge confirms that adding this eleventh paint tone officially unlocks more than 22 million unique potential configurations from the factory.
Photo: Dodge Jailbreak buyers ordering a Sub-Zero Durango can mix and match a massive factory catalog. They can go for matte-finish tinted dual stripes, five distinct brake caliper colors, and a generous list of fatory wheel designs, including the returning bronze Brass Monkey package.
In the meantime, Dodge offers custom interior leather options, such as Petrol Blue or Red stitching, exclusive materials, and custom badging combinations, so you’ll rarely see two Dodge Durango Jailbreak-customized models that look alike.
The arrival of the Sub-Zero marks the fourth consecutive month that Dodge has introduced a new factory color for the Durango. Dodge brought the Redeye in August and the After Dark in September. October was the month of the stealthy matte Smokescreen, while November has just delivered the Sub-Zero.
These four new entries bring the total 2027 model-year exterior lineup to 11 distinct paint options. The other remaining colors anchoring the lineup are B5 Blue, Destroyer Grey, Green Machine, Night Moves, Pitch Black, Red Oxide, and White Knuckle.
Photo: Dodge Unlike the Charger, where the new Sub-Zero demands a $795 premium over MSRP, ordering the new paint on the 2027 Durango costs $595 across the entire lineup. The paint is already available for all the HEMI-powered Durangos.
This means that it can become an option for those who want to go home with the Durango powered by the 5.7-liter HEMI V8, the 6.4-liter HEMI V8, or the almighty 6.2-liter supercharged HEMI V8, which cranks out 710 horsepower (720 metric horsepower). The HEMI lineup starts at $43,675. The SRT Jailbreak Hellcat is an $80,990 deal.
Last year, the aging Dodge Durango single-handedly carried the brand on its shoulders, accounting for nearly 80% of all Dodge vehicles sold nationwide. In fact, the Durango posted its best individual sales year since 2005, despite the automaker’s figures dropping by 28% compared to 2024.
Dodge sold 81,168 Durangos in 2025, with the Hornet coming in second with only 9,365. The electric Dodge Charger Daytona rounded out the podium with 7,421 units moved last year. This year, things haven’t changed much for the Durango, which was selected by 61,330 customers from January to September.

source_document.body:
Esterhazy is Mosaic’s the world’s largest potash operation. ( Image courtesy of Mosaic. )
By: Staff Writer November 4, 2026
Mosaic (NYSE: MOS) says production at its Esterhazy potash operations in Saskatchewan remained uninterrupted after a mining-induced tremor struck a mined-out area of its K3 underground mine on Tuesday.
The event occurred at 7:04 a.m. CST on Nov. 3, about 6 km east-northeast of Esterhazy, according to Earthquakes Canada , which now lists its magnitude at 3.5. All employees were accounted for and safety inspections were completed, Mosaic said.
“Mining induced seismic activity in this area is common, and our facilities are engineered with seismic loading in mind,” Mosaic said. “While the recent event occurred far from current mining areas and presents no immediate safety concerns, we continue to advance our understanding of the geological properties of the K3 ore body and will work with external experts to review seismic activity.”
The incident comes as Mosaic grapples with geological challenges at Esterhazy that have already weighed on potash production. On Tuesday, the company reported lower-than-expected ore grades at Esterhazy and reduced its 2026 potash production forecast to 8.6 million tonnes from about 9 million, a cut of roughly 4.4%.
Seismic history
It’s not the first time the Esterhazy area experiences mining-related tremors.
A worker died in a fall of ground at K3 on Dec. 15, 2025. Mosaic temporarily halted mining and announced an investigation at the time.
Esterhazy Esterhazy is one of Mosaic’s key potash production centres, with a nameplate capacity of 7.8 million tonnes annually. Mining shifted to K3 in 2021, when underground operations at K1 and K2 closed. K3 supplies ore by conveyor to the K1 and K2 processing plants.
About 1,200 people work above and below ground at Esterhazy, according to Mosaic’s website.
Production pressures
Mosaic posted a third-quarter net loss of $72 million (C$100.8 million), or 23¢ per share, compared with net income of $411 million, or $1.29 per share, a year earlier. Revenue fell about 10% to $3.1 billion.
Potash sales declined to $643 million from $695 million as volumes slipped to 2.1 million tonnes from 2.3 million tonnes.
The company attributed lower potash output to ore grades at Esterhazy and routine maintenance shutdowns at Colonsay and Belle Plaine. It expects grades to improve over time.
Muriate of potash cash production costs fell to $73 per tonne from $84 in the second quarter, although they remained above the year-earlier $71. Higher operating rates at Esterhazy and Colonsay improved fixed-cost absorption.
Mosaic is forecasting fourth-quarter potash sales of 2.3 million to 2.6 million tonnes. Realized mine-gate prices are projected to range between $255 and $275 per tonne.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s government is courting mining investment with a push to cut red tape, while developers face financing, infrastructure and permitting hurdles that can stall new operations.
Those challenges framed discussions at the Mineral Resources Review 2026 conference in St. John’s, where mining executives, investors and government officials gathered to discuss the province’s mineral potential. “They’ll tell us exactly what they want,” FireFly Metals CEO Darren Cooke told The Northern Miner at the event, describing cooperation with provincial regulators. “They’ll review some of the work before we formally submit it to give feedback.”
Closer cooperation with regulators could help developers avoid costly delays as countries compete to secure critical minerals supplies. source_document.body:
5G Edge
Qualcomm and Starlink logos displayed against a night sky, illustrating the partnership for SpaceX's nationwide terrestrial 5G network.
Qualcomm announced today that SpaceX has selected its Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms to power Starlink Mobile’s U.S. nationwide terrestrial 5G network. The multi-year agreement covers tens of thousands of base station sites, with rollout planned to begin in 2027.
Qualcomm Dragonwing QRU100 and QDU100 Platforms
Starlink Mobile will deploy Massive MIMO radio units using 64 transmit and 64 receive paths (64T64R). That is a high-capacity antenna configuration designed to improve coverage, capacity, and spectral efficiency across the terrestrial network. The Dragonwing QRU100 platform provides highly integrated processing for these Massive MIMO radio units, supporting the radio functions behind that architecture. The Dragonwing QDU100 platform handles high-performance, efficient, latency-sensitive Layer 1 processing. It also sounds like Qualcomm is providing the L1 software for this deployment. That also means it sounds like the L2 and up are being handled by something else.
Qualcomm Investor Day 2026 FY29 Growth Large
Qualcomm says the two platforms together are designed to improve performance per watt across both radio and distributed-unit processing. That energy efficiency improves network deployment economics when rolling out tens of thousands of sites. For a nationwide buildout, power draw at each location compounds quickly, and many tower sites face significant power constraints.
Final Words
This is a significant win for Qualcomm’s Dragonwing infrastructure portfolio, which has been deployed in places like Asia but, from what we gather, has not been as popular in the US. It sounds like SpaceX plans to roll out the terrestrial network alongside its satellite constellation, giving Starlink Mobile a path to become a 4th major carrier in the US. The 2027 rollout start under a multi-year agreement means tens of thousands of sites will take time to deploy nationwide. Maybe the most interesting part will be whether SpaceX can accelerate deployment of its 5G network, as it has with its AI compute build-out.

Dealer Buys a 1964 Plymouth Barracuda V8 Landau for $23,000, Flips It for $64,000 35 Days Later
31 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
This 1964 Plymouth Barracuda V8 Landau nearly tripled its value in just 35 days. The street-legal prototype was acquired by a dealer in late September. The dealer didn’t waste any time and immediately listed it for sale. Just over a month later, it sold for triple the price the dealer had paid for it. This might be the best story about classic car flipping in history.
In early 1964, Plymouth rushed to release the Barracuda, based on the compact A-body Valiant platform. It was April 1, and it somehow undercut the Ford Mustang to the market by a mere two weeks. The pony car was set to debut on April 17.
Despite beating Ford to the punch and technically starting the pony car segment, the Barracuda was initially overshadowed. The Mustang simply stole the show, selling 126,538 units before Ford switched to the 1965 model year. During the same period of 1964, Plymouth sold only 23,443 Barracudas .
On the Mustang's very first opening weekend, over 22,000 customers placed an order, nearly matching the figures of the Barracuda for the entire 1964. But before things took off, Chrysler's styling and engineering experts pulled a standard, early-production V8 Barracuda off the production line and used it to experiment with design.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The styling division implemented several bespoke modifications that set it apart from any other Barracuda ever built. The designers sectioned the roof, installing a custom-engineered, removable fabric panel over the front passengers, creating a unique, semi-open-air targa or town-car effect.
The studio also added thick vinyl accents, custom chrome badges, and specialized exterior brightwork, all in the name of premium Landau styling. The removable fabric top panel of the prototype is still functional but shows its age, requiring careful alignment when latching. The listing says it doesn’t even fit properly on the Plymouth.
The prototype retains its highly authentic, early Mopar A-body mechanical architecture, which makes it exceptionally reliable and pretty straightforward to service. Under the hood sits a 273-cubic-inch (4.5-liter) LA V8 engine with a Carter two-barrel carburetor, factory-rated at 180 horsepower (183 metric horsepower).
A three-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission, operated via Chrysler's iconic dashboard push-buttons positioned to the left of the steering wheel, puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure pony car fashion. 1964 was the final year for this design. Power-assisted drums at each corner provide the stopping power. The brake master cylinder has been replaced recently.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Automakers usually crush developmental prototypes to avoid liability issues. However, Chrysler allowed this one vehicle to enter private hands once its styling evaluations were completed. This is how the prototype survived intact for the following 60 years.
Painted from the factory in metallic gold, often referred to as Barracuda Gold Poly, paint code AA-1, and sporting a color-coordinated gold and black interior, this car comes from an era when big wheels weren’t even a thing: it rides on 13-inch (yes, you read that right) wheels with styled wheel covers and National Horizon polyester whitewall tires.
Huge front bucket seats with lap belts offer lounge-like comfort for the driver and front passenger, but the driver's seat shows the normal signs of wear and tear. The distinct fold-down rear seats create a seven-foot cargo space. The three-spoke steering wheel frames a speedometer scaled up to 110 mph (177 kph). The gauges indicating the fuel level and coolant temperature are inoperative.
The odometer reads 52,446 miles (84,404 kilometers) and, as expected from a vintage vehicle that has been driven instead of garage-queened, it is starting to show its age. It sports light paint chips and normal undercarriage road wear, but it remains free of structural rust.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The prototype is street-legal, it runs, drives, stops, and holds a clean Tennessee title. That is what the buyer paid $64,000 for, along with a motorized password to car shows. It could be the beginning of a life in the spotlight for the 1964 Plymouth Barracuda V8 Landau prototype .
It has been a bumpy ride for the vehicle so far, as it crossed the block several times. Back in September 2010, when it was auctioned by RM Sotheby’s at Auburn Fall, the bidding did not meet the reserve, and the car did not sell.
The V8-powered Landau came out of storage once again in 2026, when the previous owner auctioned it off in Nashville at the Mecum event. A licensed dealer paid $23,100 to trailer it to its showroom, located in Marine City, Michigan.
The dealer did not waste much time and, less than a month later, listed it for sale on Bring a Trailer. The prototype stole the show on the platform and bidding instantly took off. The prototype spent a week online and the hammer dropped at $64,000, nearly tripling the seller’s investment in just 35 days. Now that’s car flipping at its best!

5 Water-Coooled Porsche 911s So Rare That Most Will Never See One in the Wild
35 photos
Photo: Porsche AG
For what used to be a large part of the Porsche 911 enthusiast community, 1997 is the year where the story ended. That is when the water-cooled 996 generation was introduced to replace the more old-school, air-cooled 993, forever changing the 911 lineage going forward.
Details like an all-new platform, a new generation of water-cooled flat-sixes and a set of headlights that everyone compared to runny fried eggs made the majority of 911 fans to consider the 996 as a huge downgrade, and the beginning of the end for the lovable nameplate. Some of those purists, very few of which remain, are still saying the same thing three decades later.
Oddly enough, the used car market has been in complete agreement with those very few remaining Porsche purists, which is probably why air-cooled 911s still command gigantic prices compared to other sports cars from their eras. The 993 in particular now has the status of the last car from a lost golden age.
It’s not all bad, though, because, even with the somewhat lackluster reception for the 996, some of the water-cooled 911s unveiled since have managed to achieve legendary status as well. One of the main reasons for that can be found in one of Porsche’s decade’s old tradition of building racing cars and then selling road-going versions of said cars in very low numbers.
It didn’t take much for the Zuffenhausen carmaker to discover that scarcity can be a great marketing strategy, and those low-volume 911s can both fill its coffers and the image of the brand at the same time. Starting with the 996 generation and intensifying with every one that followed, Porsche’s motorsport engineers in Weissach, or its GT division, began developing 911s that were built in deliberately small numbers. Augmenting them were also special one-offs and limited edition models from Porsche Exclusive Manufaktur, but those have existed since 1986, back in the air-cooled era.
Taking a step back, it’s pretty obvious that the rarest but still mass-produced 911s from the water-cooled era are some of the most coveted Porsches. Despite many of them being developed by the GT division, they are not necessarily the fastest 911s, nor the most expensive, albeit several of them are both.
Some of them used a manual transmission despite the PDK dual-clutch making them much quicker, others had most of their sound insulation replaced with lightweight materials, while others stubbornly kept more old-school naturally aspirated flat-sixes instead of switching to the more modern turbocharged technology that took over the rest of the 911 lineup.
All in all, all these limited edition 911s are part of a parallel history of the water-cooled 911s, and when you draw the line they have very few things in common with most of the Porsches you see on the street. With that in mind, I decided to gather some of the rarest and most impressive 911s from each generation of the modern water-cooled era, whether they were just homologation specials, tributes to a long-forgotten golden age, or simply a more analog love-letter to being slightly different in a world that is increasingly more digital.
Porsche 911 GT3 RS (996): The Fried Eggs That Grew Teeth After the 996 generation was unveiled in 1997, it instantly became the 911 that all those Porsche purists love to hate. It had switched to an all-new platform for the first time, which it shared with the Boxster, it had water-cooling, and a set of headlights that were mocked for looking like a pair of runny fried eggs. For years it was seen as the most embarrassing generation of the 911, and if you also add the less than ideal reliability figures, it’s not surprising that the used car market has treated them rather poorly compared to other generations.
That said, Porsche developed a mid-cycle facelift and a bunch of more hardcore versions that made most of those problems seem a bit irrelevant. Unveiled in 2003, the 996 GT3 RS was the first 911 to have the GT3 RS moniker, making it the origin of the most hardcore, track-ready versions of the Neunelfer lineage.
Photo: Porsche AG Built as an homologation special, its original raison d’etre was to bring Porsche’s 911 racing cars in line with FIA rules, and that reason couldn’t be more evident the more you looked at it. Under the short engine cover, which was adorned with an FIA-spec wing, sat a naturally aspirated, 3.6-liter “Mezger” flat-six. It was part of a legendary engine family named after its designer, Hans Mezger, and it delivered 381 PS (376 HP).
Surprisingly, that is the same official output as the non-RS 996.2 GT3, albeit the two engines were mildly different. Unlike the facelifted GT3, the first 911 GT3 RS’s flat-six featured a reshaped intake design whose opening acted as a ram-air system, modified cylinder heads, and a differently shaped exhaust port for race homologation purposes. Allegedly, these measures gave it around 400 horsepower on the dyno.
Other differences compared to the regular GT3 were a lighter flywheel and a 50 kg (110 pounds) weight reduction, all of which gave the RS a 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration of 4.2 seconds compared to the 4.5 seconds required by the 996.2 GT3. Only 682 were ever built, making it far rarer than the 997.1 GT3 RS that followed.
Porsche 911 Sport Classic (997): The Return of the Ducktail While the 996 GT3 RS was the first water-cooled 911’s track warrior, the limited-edition 997 Sport Classic had a more romantic reason for existence. Unveiled at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show, it was the first nostalgic 911 in an era when Porsche was becoming increasingly known for smashing lap times than winning beauty pageants. Unsurprisingly, all 250 that were ever built were sold out in just 48 hours, and it was all down to what the Sport Classic stood for.
The model was developed by Porsche Exclusive Manufaktur to celebrate the customization department's return to crafting bespoke vehicle projects in limited numbers. It was meant to be a rolling tribute to the special 911s of the early 1970s, with the fixed ducktail spoiler clearly referencing the Carrera RS 2.7.
Photo: Porsche AG Other retro design details consisted of the 19-inch alloys inspired by the old-school Fuchs, while the double-bubble roof clearly gave a nod to the Carrera GT and racing Porsches. Who would need the design to clear more space for the passengers’ helmets.
Despite being rear-wheel-drive only, the 997 Sport Classic was technically based on the wider Carrera 4S body, which gave it a more muscular stance without the added weight of an AWD system. Under the ducktail sat the 3.8-liter flat-six from the Carrera S, but upgraded with the so-called Porsche Powerkit, which included polished combustion chambers, a revised intake, a new exhaust system and a remapped ECU.
These modifications increased its output from 385 PS (380 HP) to 408 PS (402 HP), which was sent to the rear wheels through a short-shift six-speed manual only. It also came standard with ceramic brakes, lowered PASM suspension and a limited-slip differential. All in all, it was one of the very few water-cooled 911s that was built to be both admired and driven.
Porsche 911 GT2 RS (997): The Modern Widowmaker Made in Nissan’s Spite Apparently, Porsche’s development code name for the first-ever GT2 RS was “Project 727,” which wasn’t just a random number, but actually referenced the 7.26.7 minutes lap time set at the time by the Nissan GT-R (R35). Porsche’s GT department took that lap time personally, which is why the 911 GT2 RS lapped the Nordschleife in just 7.18 minutes, completely demolishing all other production sports cars at the time.
Upon its debut, the model was the most powerful street-legal Porsche of all time, with its twin-turbocharged, 3.6-liter flat-six delivering no less than 620 PS (612 HP) and 700 Nm (516 lb-ft) of torque. Even more impressive, and what gave it the “modern widowmaker” nickname, was that all that oomph was sent exclusively to the rear wheels through a six-speed manual gearbox.
Photo: Porsche AG Despite being clearly developed for track domination, the first-ever 911 GT2 RS had no AWD and no PDK transmission on the options list, making it the most powerful manual-transmission model Porsche had built up to that point. The weight loss compared to the “regular” 911 GT2 was equally impressive, since it weighed just 1,370 kg (3,021 pounds), or 70 kg less than the car it replaced.
The 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration took just 3.5 seconds, 200 kph (124 mph) was reached in under 10 seconds, and despite the extra downforce it also sported a 330 kph (205 mph) top speed. The low weight, motorsport-derived aerodynamic and high output made it quicker on track than any other hypercars of its time, including the Bugatti Veyron.
Compared to all the GT2 RS models that followed, the original one was by far the rarest, with only 500 units having been built, and the only one to exclusively feature a manual transmission, making it the holy grail of track-ready, turbocharged 911s.
Porsche 911 GT3 RS 4.0 (997): The Last Mezger Engine In many ways, the 911 GT3 RS 4.0 was the final evolution of the 997 generation, and it also takes honors as the final Porsche using the race-derived Mezger flat-six. For that reason, many saw it as a GT3 built around the engine, and the 600 units that were ever built made it even more legendary.
That engine was a 3,996 cc flat-six, the largest ever fitted to a street-legal 911 up to that point. Porsche’s GT department had lengthened the stroke from 76.4 mm to 80.4 mm, also borrowing the exact same crankshaft from the GT3 RSR racing car. The model also had titanium connecting rods and forged pistons, with the result being 500 PS (493 HP) at a stratospheric 8,250 rpm.
Photo: Porsche AG This translated into a specific output of more than 123 HP per liter, which was massive for a naturally aspirated engine of that size. The rest of the car was, once again, a lesson in weight-savings, with a carbon fiber hood and front wings, racing bucket seats, plastic rear windows and even weight-optimized carpets. All these measures gave it a weight of just 1,360 kg (2,998 pounds) with a full tank.
Aerodynamics were incredible as well, with just the front winglets adding another 190 kg (419 pounds) of downforce at top speed. Speaking of which, the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) sprint took just 3.9 seconds, despite the car being RWD and manual-only, while top speed was 310 kph (193 mph)/.
Oddly enough despite less horsepower and a lot less torque, it managed a 7 minutes and 27 seconds Nordschleife lap time, which was identical to the time set by the Nissan GT-R a few years earlier. It is now the last manual-only GT3 RS.
Porsche 911 R (991): The Special Edition That Taught Porsche a Lesson The 911 R nameplate was originally used on an homologation special from 1967 that never quite became one. Porsche built just 23 of them after realizing that selling the 500 units needed for homologation couldn’t be made in a profitable manner. The resulting cars had their competition careers relegated to non-production classes only, but they became legends anyway.
Almost half a century later, Porsche’s GT department revived the nameplate but with a different thought in mind, and that was to prove that a manual gearbox and a naturally aspirated engine still made sense in the modern 911 lineup. It also inadvertently fed a lot of sports car scalpers, and indirectly birthed the 992 GT3 Touring as a production model.
Photo: Porsche AG Unveiled at the 2016 Geneva Motor Show, the modern 911 R (991) used a rather simple formula. It received the GT3 RS’ 4.0-liter naturally aspirated flat-six, which delivered 500 PS (493 HP) and 8,250 rpm, a newly developed six-speed manual with an optional lightweight single-mass flywheel, and then removed pretty much every comfort feature that wasn’t essential for driving.
At just 1,370 kg (3,020 pounds), it was 50 kg lighter than the PDK-only 911 GT3 RS (991), and this was made possible by the addition of carbon-fiber front fenders, polycarbonate rear windows, a magnesium roof, and a titanium exhaust system.
In short, it was a lighter, more analog GT3 RS, and without any flamboyant wings and spoilers. On top of it, Porsche limited it to just 991 units, as a nod to the 911 generation internal codename, and all of them were sold even before the first car was ever built. Sadly, a lot of them were bought by scalpers who then re-sold them for much more money, and this is probably what gave Porsche the idea of making the non-limited 911 GT3 Touring (992), which is pretty much just a more gentleman-looking GT3.
